summary: Subaccount migration + background heartbeat causing tenant 429s on Dedicated pool
description:
Issue summary:
Customer reports a sudden increase in 429 rejections after performing a subaccount split/migration while a background snapshot restore and heartbeat system were active. The customer is on a Dedicated pool in eu-west and observed tenant-wide soft 429 waves starting immediately after the migration.

Impact:
- Production traffic for NovaHealth (dedicated) receiving intermittent 429s across chat and embedding routes.
- Degraded throughput for customer-facing workflows; several short-lived sessions saw repeated early rejects.
- Customer reports user-facing errors in health-monitoring dashboards and a small SLO breach for the last 24h.

Environment:
- Dedicated pool: dp-326-eu-west (reserved capacity)
- Region: eu-west (calls routed also to us-east failover)
- Customer config: subaccount split (old_org -> new_org), signed URL callbacks, keepalive-enabled SSE ingest for telemetry heartbeats and restore process triggering periodic callbacks.

Steps to reproduce (as reported by customer):
1) Start background snapshot restore job from object-store (scheduled) which issues routine HEAD callbacks to the Redwood signed URL callback endpoints every 10s per worker.
2) Trigger subaccount split migration using our console (moves 50 subaccounts under a new parent).
3) Observe increased 429s across interactive chat endpoints and bulk-embedding endpoints for ~10-30 minutes.

Observed behavior:
- Early 429s with throttle headers: x-rw-retry-after present but inconsistent.
- Console shows tenant token consumption jumping in short bursts correlated with the restore job heartbeats.
- Rate-limiter logs show duplicate token accounting for the same signed-url callback under two different route fingerprints (origin header vs. rewritten X-Forwarded-User).

Expected behavior:
- Background heartbeats and signed-url callbacks should be counted against a background/burst pool or be treated as low-cost probes if configured; subaccount migration should not double-count identical callbacks nor cause tenant-level refill drift.

Additional context:
- Customer upgraded to a higher tier during the migration window (commit refresh) but 429s persisted.
- Customer uses an edge proxy that rewrites some headers for multitenancy and also has a healthcheck probe collector running in us-east.

Relevant logs & links:
- Rate-limiter ledger snapshot (redact): https://logs.redwood.ai/tenant/NovaHealth/rl-ledger/2026-03-03-08:23
- Edge proxy request traces (sample): https://tracing.redwood.ai/trace/8a1f2df
- Support Slack thread: #support-novahealth (https://redwood.slack.com/archives/C05NOVAHD)

Immediate ask from customer:
- Explain why 429s started during migration and whether there is a config change or workaround to prevent further user impact.
comments: 2026-03-03 09:12 - Camila Ruiz (Customer): We started the migration and saw 429s within ~3 minutes. The restore job was still running; can you confirm whether the callback pattern is expected to spike token accounting?

2026-03-03 09:30 - Support (Liam Chen): Thanks Camila — triaging now. Can you share an example request-id from a rejected request so we can correlate with rate-limiter traces? Also attaching ledger snapshot request.

2026-03-03 11:02 - Customer (Camila Ruiz): Sample rejected request-id: req_20260303_8a1f2df; attached a short pcap and proxy config excerpt. Note: proxy injects X-Forwarded-User header for subaccount routing.

2026-03-03 14:48 - SRE (Ethan Brooks): Initial findings: rate-limiter shows two route fingerprints for the same signed-url callback. One fingerprint includes origin host, the other includes X-Forwarded-User. This leads to double token accounting on some bursts.

2026-03-04 08:15 - Support (Liam Chen): Temporary mitigation suggested: pause background restore job or set it to a slower cadence while we investigate; alternatively we can enable a short-lived split-burst-pool for background probes if desired. Customer agreed to pause the restore job at 08:40 UTC.

2026-03-09 16:20 - Engineering (Maya Singh): We reproduced header-fingerprint divergence in staging by replaying signed-url callbacks through the edge-proxy with header rewrite. Filing infra follow-up to make route fingerprinting ignore X-Forwarded-User for signed callbacks.
investigation_notes:
Summary of debug steps performed:
- Correlated request-ids with rate-limiter ledger and edge traces; found duplicate ledger increments for same request_id under two fingerprints.
- Reviewed proxy rewrite rules: edge-proxy rewrites X-Forwarded-User and also strips/rewrites Host for origin routing; that produced two distinct route keys in the rate-limiter.
- Checked dedicated pool autoscaler: no scale events during the window. Not a capacity shortage but an accounting anomaly.
- Cross-region healthcheck collector in us-east was replaying the same signed callback during the split leading to near-synchronous duplicate requests counted separately by regional ingress.
Hypothesis: combination of (a) header rewrite at edge, (b) subaccount split causing duplicate signed-url routing, and (c) cross-region probe replay produced transient double-counting and refill drift, triggering soft 429 waves.
Next steps: engineering to adjust fingerprinting rules to ignore transient headers for signed callbacks, and add a mitigation in rate-limiter to dedupe per-request-id within a short window. Evidence links: trace and ledger links in description.
resolution: Workaround applied and recommended: customer paused the background restore job and reduced heartbeat cadence to 60s; we enabled a temporary burst pool isolation for NovaHealth so interactive traffic recovered. Engineering change in progress: update route fingerprinting to ignore X-Forwarded-User for signed callbacks and add per-request-id dedupe. Final fix ETA: engineering estimates 5 business days. Pending follow-up: confirm post-fix with a small migration rehearsal.
